messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Caleb is a 26-year-old detective, married, who presented for psychological evaluation following a prolonged period of physical abuse perpetrated by his former romantic partner prior to his current marriage. He scored a 72 on the PCL-5, indicating severe posttraumatic symptomatology. The abuse had unfolded across nearly two years and was characterised by escalating violence — his partner would drink heavily before attacks, and the smell of alcohol on her breath had become, for Caleb, the sensory herald of what was coming. She had targeted his body methodically, leaving bruises and lacerations that he had learned to conceal beneath long sleeves at work. The sounds of her voice during those episodes — a particular low, controlled tone she used just before striking him — had burned themselves into his memory in ways he could not yet fully articulate when he first sat down with the clinician.

In the months after leaving that relationship and entering his current marriage, Caleb found that the world had not simply reset. The memories of the abuse were vivid and detailed in a way that felt almost hallucinatory — he could recall the specific quality of light in the apartment, the texture of the floor beneath him, and most disturbingly, he could hear her voice in his head with a clarity that made him doubt, momentarily, that he was alone. These memories were not retrieved voluntarily; they forced themselves into his awareness without permission, arriving most violently when something in his environment carried a trace of the past. The smell of alcohol — encountered regularly when Caleb interviews suspects or processes scenes involving intoxicated individuals — would hit him and the memory would open like a wound, auditory and visual and visceral all at once. Seeing injuries on others, which as a detective he encounters with grim regularity at crime scenes, carried the same detonating quality. Even nausea, arising from stress or fatigue, was enough to pull him back — his body had learned to read its own distress as a signal of danger, and the memory would arrive uninvited. These triggers did not merely surface the past; they confirmed something darker. Each intrusion reinforced his growing conviction that people are not what they seem, that the person who had claimed to love him had hidden cruelty beneath familiarity, and that this kind of concealment was not exceptional but structural to human relationships. He had lost his faith — not in any formal religious sense, but in the basic legibility of other people and in the idea that ordinary life could be safe. He felt, increasingly, like a permanent outsider, someone who had been inducted into a knowledge that others did not carry and that separated him irrevocably from them.

These appraisals, once settled, fed back into the memory itself. Believing that people are fundamentally unknowable made the past feel not like an aberration but like a revelation, and the memories returned with the added weight of that meaning — more frequent, more confirming, more difficult to metabolise. In response, Caleb had developed a set of strategies that had accumulated quietly over months. He had stopped allowing himself to relax, reasoning — with a logic that made complete sense to him — that the moments he had been most hurt were moments when he had been unguarded. He numbed his emotional responses with a deliberateness he had come to think of as professional composure. He avoided being touched, which had created a visible and painful distance from his wife, who had begun to ask questions he did not know how to answer. These strategies, however, had begun to generate their own costs. The hypervigilance required to never fully relax meant his body remained in a state of chronic arousal, and that arousal itself — the nausea it produced, the hypersensitivity to sensory input — became a trigger in its own right, pulling the memory forward again. The numbing and the withdrawal, meanwhile, deepened his sense of being an outsider, confirming to him that he was no longer capable of ordinary connection, which only hardened his distrust and his loss of faith.

What finally brought Caleb to seek help was a moment at work. He had been interviewing a domestic violence survivor and found himself unable to continue — not because of professional inadequacy, but because he had begun to shake. His wife had found him that evening sitting in the car in the driveway for forty minutes, unable to come inside. He told the clinician he was most afraid that nothing would ever feel safe again — and most hoping, quietly, that he was wrong.
